newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel and Syria swap messages, Levy says.
newsitem.headline: Israel and Syria swap messages, Levy says.

text.p: Israel's Foreign Minister David Levy said on Wednesday he was exchanging messages with Damascus indirectly and appealed to his Syrian counterpart to meet him to revive peace talks.

The Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported earlier in the day that Levy and Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara had been exchanging messages through a senior European cabinet minister. It did not identify the middleman.

"I hope the things which Syria in fact intends in its strategy -- the way it is passed to me -- is peace. So the messages I am passing are with this aim," Levy told Israel Radio when asked about the newspaper report.
He declined to publicly discuss "a single detail" of the exchange.
On-again, off-again peace talks that began in 1991 have been stuck over the fate of the Golan Heights captured by Israel from Syria in the 1967 Middle East war.

Speaking later in Jerusalem to foreign ambassadors, Levy appealed to his Syrian counterpart directly: "Please sir, as representatives of two countries that want peace...please, please, anywhere, at any hour, I am ready to meet you.

"Together we'll prepare for the meeting of our leaders, of teams from the two sides and we'll sit and we will deserve the responsibility that falls on our shoulders in this generation," Levy said in the appeal to Shara.
Haaretz said European officials hoped to bring Levy and Shara together in April at a meeting of foreign ministers to further a joint Middle Eastern, North African and European cooperative effort.
The Israeli pullback from most of the West Bank town of Hebron last week has revived peace moves with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and interest in the long-stalled talks with Syria.

Syria demands the return of all of the Golan Heights but Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected any withdrawal from the strategic plateau that towers over surrounding areas of Syria and Israel.

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk appealed to Syria and Lebanon on Tuesday to use Hebron as a springboard to further peacemaking. He said Jordan, Egypt, Morocco and Oman had already shown signs of a thaw in ties with Israel.

"When Yasser Arafat calls Bibi Netanyahu his friend and partner, then why shouldn't the others do the same?" Indyk told the Foreign Press Association. On Wednesday, Indyk said Israel, Syria and Lebanon had to find formulas for resuming their talks.

A spokesman for Netanyahu said on Sunday the Israeli leader, elected in May, was prepared to resume talks with Syria, suspended about a year ago, without preconditions. Previous talks were based on the concept of Israel trading occupied Arab land for peace.
Israel's previous Labour-led government, ousted by Netanyahu, broke off talks with Syria in March 1996 after Islamic suicide bombings in Israel killed 59 people.
The Arab world questioned Netanyahu's commitment to peace following his election on a promise to bolster Israeli security and to oppose swapping occupied Arab land for peace.
Syrian Prime Minister Mahmoud Zu'bi slammed Netanyahu on Monday, saying: "There is no other option but for Israel's unconditional withdrawal from the Golan."
